After looking at storage speeds and other things, it seemed like I should just skip 10 Gigabit altogether (cheaper to get additional faster NVMe SSD drives for local devices). And the AC wifi is completely sufficient for my needs. Upgrades won't be needed until all the ISP's finally start offering >1GbE at home. Who knows how many years it will take. cs.th: Bad times in corporate wireless networks

cs.t: I've been using MT gear for about 10 years now. I actually think the devices themselves are very solid once they're up and running. I've had some running for years without any issues (try that with most other SOHO router brands!), though reboots are much more frequent these days due to security updates. I do agree though that the software side of things can be a bit quirky and the recent security issues are a worrying glimpse into the quality of their code. In general I wish the platform was more open (you can't even get a shell without rooting the device), but it's something I can live with at this price point. Unfortunately given their affordability and feature set, Mikrotik routers are often times administered by people who don't really have a solid grasp of networking. I've seen some downright awful advice posted on their user forums over the years, stuff that could easily cause connectivity issues under the right circumstances. Who knows how much of that gets copy/pasted into configs after a quick Google search.
cs.th: MikroTik routers are forwarding owners’ traffic to unknown attackers

cs.t: What vulnerabilities would you imagine there to be in an unmanaged (aka: dumb) switch? Someone can force the switch to flood all traffic to all ports? Bearing in mind that switches generally have special-purpose hardware that's responsible for handling switching, I find it unlikely that cheapass dumbswitches have enough CPU to copy LAN data and send it out to a remote system at any useful speed. Also, next time you're looking for a switch (or if you're still within the return period for your used switch), consider Mikrotik switches. I've had four CRS326-24G-2S+ units for three, maybe five years now and I'm quite happy with them. However, I know nothing about their routers or WiFi APs.

cs.t: The Mikrotik switch is awesome, and it's still the most compact 10G switch available. You can fix the thermal issue either by adding a small fan (Noctua is great) or by adding more radiators:  https://pics.ealex.net/share/UxeSf_AWHLIuc-qzK5zl7JIgQvQDAZh...  I've been running it like this in a closed comm box for the last 3 years without any issues. SFP+ modules actually do not use that much power, it's just that it's concentrated into a small package, resulting in high temps.

cs.t: Good to know since I was thinking of using it as an access point.

I have hap ax3. They cleaned up their defaults. No extra license costs. One issue I had was that I was affected (and many others) by wifi bug in firmware which made connections drop randomly. Took them half a year to resolve it. Wouldn't recommend Mikrotik as access point. Otherwise it's good.

- 1430.3 Mbps for 25 ip filter rules in a 70€ Wi-Fi 7 router doesn't sound that bad to me. Also, as sibling comment says, you can enable fast tracking for certain connections. - Mikrotik doesn't have open ports to the outside since years and years ago, IIRC. They had a CVE on their administration port (not in ssh) in 2023, but you shouldn't open that port to the outside anyway. - All Mikrotik wireless routers include at least a level 4 license. You only need a higher license level if you need more than 200 VPN tunnels or more than 200 users in the hotspot functionality. A bigger wireless router like the hAP ax³ will already have a level 6 license, the biggest one. You might need a license if you set up a Mikrotik instance in a X86 server, or virtualized, for example to manage a bigger site or as a bigger hotspot controller. Licenses aren't expensive and are paid only once, no subscriptions (by device, I think you get a device ID or something like that). - All the Mikrotik routers that I own still get updates. The RB750GL, that was released like 15 years ago or more, still updated.
I have a 10gbit LAN running over fiber with Mikrotik switches and cheapo Intel NICs. Works fine, and it makes remote disks quite a bit nicer than when they are over 1gbit.

cs.t: Nice score on the used switch! I used a 10GbE Mikrotik up until recently until it started having hardware failures (my second one, a few years older is running perfectly, been very happy with it). I got exceptionally lucky finding a used 64 port 40/100Gbps enterprise switch on ebay for $1000CAD (same switch here normally goes for $3-4k CAD used). Most of my ceph cluster is limited to 10Gbps (onboard RJ45 for 4/5 nodes, and the PCI-E slot on each is taken by NVMe drives), but I feel I'm already outgrowing that speed, my few nodes already saturate 10Gbps - NVMe drives are fast! Now I just gotta wait for 100GbE NICs to come down in price, I'm not sure I'm ready to buy a used NIC yet (was nervous about the switch, first used piece of network gear for me), but the knock off Intels are like $350 minimum here for a 2 port.
